drug_class: Adenosine receptor antagonist (A2A blocker) — Parkinson's disease add-on therapy
purpose: Istradefylline is used to help people with Parkinson's disease who are already taking levodopa/carbidopa but still experience periods when their medication seems to 'wear off' and their symptoms return. It helps reduce those 'off' periods — the times when you feel stiff, slow, or have more difficulty moving. It is used as an add-on treatment, not a replacement for your current Parkinson's medicines.
how_it_works: In your brain, there is a chemical signal called adenosine that can block the pathways that help control your movements. Istradefylline works by blocking a specific adenosine receptor called A2A, which helps those movement pathways work more smoothly. Think of it like removing a roadblock so your brain's movement signals can flow more freely, helping your levodopa medicine work better and longer.
common_side_effects: Uncontrolled, involuntary movements (dyskinesia), dizziness, constipation, nausea, hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), trouble sleeping, and feeling confused. Some people may also notice changes in mood or impulse control.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you experience any new or unusual urges (like gambling, spending, or sexual urges), as istradefylline may cause impulse control problems. It can cause or worsen hallucinations and confusion, especially in older patients. Do not suddenly stop taking this medicine without talking to your doctor. Avoid smoking, as it can lower the amount of medicine in your body and make it less effective. Use caution when driving until you know how this medicine affects you.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 20 mg taken by mouth once a day. Your doctor may increase the dose to 40 mg once daily if needed. It can be taken with or without food. If you smoke cigarettes, your doctor may prescribe the higher dose since smoking reduces how much of the medicine stays in your body.
